newsitem.title: INDIA: Suicide threats, race row hit Miss World contest.
newsitem.headline: Suicide threats, race row hit Miss World contest.

text.p: Suicide threats by feminist protesters and race rows with the media have angered would-be Miss Worlds competing in India, where the beauty pageant has attracted more controversy than ever before.

A women's activist group is threatening to upstage the crowning moment on November 23 by infiltrating the crowd in Bangalore's Chinnaswamy cricket stadium, taking cyanide and setting their silk saris alight.

"I just hope everything will turn out alright. This threat of burning themselves makes me mad and sad," Miss Venezuela Anna Cepinska, the bookmakers favourite to take the title, told Reuters on Sunday.

One man committed died by self-immolation on Thursday in a protest against India hosting the beauty contest. The suicide sent shudders through the Miss World camp at the luxury Windsor Manor hotel in Bangalore.

"This is the land of Gandhi, the land of peace. How can they take such an extreme step. Everybody has a right to protest but not in this form. I am very concerned," said Miss Costa Rica, Natalia Caravjal Lorenzo, an aspiring journalist.
To add to the controversy dogging this year's Miss World, the African contingent among the 88 competitors say the media is shunning them because they are black.
"I didn't expect this kind of discrimination in India. I am really disappointed," Shose Akaro of Tanzania told Reuters at the weekend.
"The Indian press has totally ignored us (black Africans) from the day we landed in your country. Just about everyone in the press is paying attention only to the whites," she said.
Miss Zambia, law student Alice Banda who is hoping to make a career in politics after graduating, felt similarly ignored.
"Just look at them. The press are going after the whites," she said as Indian and foreign television crews and photographers closed in on white competitors.
Eric Morley, the man who started the competition 45 years ago in Britain, said this year's event had attracted more publicity than ever before, but not the sort that anybody would want.
His wife Julia, who is president of the Miss World Organisation, appealed to the womens groups for talks to defuse the situation but was turned down flat.

"It is really sad if they have to burn themselves as a mark of protest. I now learn that they only represent small groups and have just been making threats. Julia Morley has offered to discuss with them but they have not accepted the offer," said Miss America Kelly Webber.

The Mahila Jagran Samiti (Forum to Awaken Women) is holding its threat of suicides in abeyance while a court rules on a move to ban the show, which is being staged in India for the first time although Indian women have won the title twice.
A decision is expected on Monday. Previous attempts to block Miss World through the courts have failed.
"We will decide on a course of action after the judgment," Kinay Narayan Shishikala, firebrand leader of the Mahila Jagran Samiti, told Reuters at the weekend.
The Miss World opponents say the beauty contest offends Indian culture and demeans women.
"I don't know how it will change things by burning themsleves. I would have had second thoughts about coming if they had done it before we arrived," said Miss Australia Nicole Smith.
